Latest Update: Why the Northeast Could Lead a Factory-Built Housing Boom

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.
  • A new economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.
  • Recent findings suggest that berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional upcoming construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.

A new economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.

Recent findings suggest that berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional upcoming construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone. For years, people seemingly used “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” interchangeably. But they’re not the same thing.

Sources indicate that for one, the “mobile home” classification was retired in 1980, though many still use it colloquially. That year, it was replaced by the term “manufactured home.” Broadly, manufactured homes are those built in a factory and then transported to a site.

Recent findings suggest that for years, federal Housing and Urban Development code required that all manufactured homes have a permanent steel towing frame underneath. New provisions in the Road to Housing Act, meant to spur more affordable housing, eliminated that requirement.

The act further entitles these latest chassis-free homes to the same financing, titling, insurance, taxes, transport, and installation as conventional homes.

The hope is that creating this fresh category of manufactured home will help blunt one of the housing industry’s sharpest pain points: affordable starter homes.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of affordable starter homes for sale has markedly decreased.

According to recent reports, realtor.com research found roughly 300,000 fewer affordable “starter” listings on the market today than before the pandemic. The cost of those starter homes rose from $256,000 in 2019 to $344,000 in 2026. By comparison, the median price of a manufactured home in April 2026 was $134,800.

To understand what metros might see the biggest impact from this upcoming type of manufactured home, Realtor.com scored the 100 largest metro areas on three metrics: the percentage of single-family starter homes (defined as listings priced at or below 80% of the local median) in the area; the relative price-per-square-foot premiums for traditional new construction; and the availability of affordable vacant land.

Recent findings suggest that six of the 10 opportunity metros were in the Northeast, including Hartford; Allentown; Albany; Rochester, NY; Syracuse, NY; and Worcester, MA. Other metros that made the list were Denver; Colorado Springs, CO; Albuquerque, NM; and Spokane, WA.

In Hartford, which ranked first, starter homes account for just 17.9% of single-family inventory, while site-built new construction costs 29.1% more per square foot than existing homes.

Recent findings suggest that in third-ranked Allentown, single-family starter homes made up 22.9% of housing in the area, but new-construction costs were 33.6% more than existing homes. In sixth-ranked Albany, starter homes comprised 31.6% of the single-family inventory, but the price per square foot for new construction is 47% higher than for existing homes.

That’s nothing compared with seventh-ranked Rochester, where 33.7% of homes are starter but site-built new construction costs 97% more per square foot than existing homes.

Sources indicate that while the economics in these cities are compelling, another reason manufactured housing may become more popular in these metros is that frigid Northeastern winters limit conventional housing construction. Meanwhile, manufactured housing can be assembled year-round.

Before Hartford, Albany, or any other metro can begin taking advantage of the Road to Housing Act’s fresh manufactured housing rules, municipal zoning laws will need to change, Berner found.

According to Land Use Labs data cited in the report, only about 17% of zoned land nationwide explicitly permits manufactured housing communities, and many municipalities enforce minimum floor-size rules or design restrictions that block factory-built units.

Industry News: Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.
  • As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs.
  • “What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante remarked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:56 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

As inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante remarked. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”.

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:.

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”.

Memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

In a recent development, “You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”.

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

Sources indicate that “We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:.

Recent findings suggest that protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

“It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”.

Sources indicate that at Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production challenges, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

Industry observers note that “If you run a massive training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti stated during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very vital metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”.

In a recent development, for International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

Industry observers note that “This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:.

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

“We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst remarked during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:.

In a recent development, walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:.

Mountain Modern Home With Views of Two Ski Resorts Lists for $15.3 Million in Park City

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the end of a private drive in Park City, UT, a mountain modern home with views of not one but two ski resorts has come on the market for $15,250,000.
  • Designed by Aspen-based CCY Architects, the home at 15 Eagle Pointe Court balances modernist sophistication with mountain coziness, featuring Telluride Gold stonework, an oxidized Corten steel roof and Western red cedar siding.
  • "Modern lines of steel and glass are paired with warm wood finishes and natural stone, providing seamless indoor-outdoor living within a private mountain landscape," says listing agent Michael LaPay of Summit Sotheby's International Realty Park City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the end of a private drive in Park City, UT, a mountain modern home with views of not one but two ski resorts has come on the market for $15,250,000.

Designed by Aspen-based CCY Architects, the home at 15 Eagle Pointe Court balances modernist sophistication with mountain coziness, featuring Telluride Gold stonework, an oxidized Corten steel roof and Western red cedar siding.

"Modern lines of steel and glass are paired with warm wood finishes and natural stone, providing seamless indoor-outdoor living within a private mountain landscape," says listing agent Michael LaPay of Summit Sotheby's International Realty Park City.

LaPay knows the house well. He represented the original owners, who built it in 2005, and has handled its last two sales as well.

The four-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom residence spans 7,053 square feet on 2.69 acres in Park Meadows.

"This property's size and location at the end of a private drive is a rarity in the coveted Park Meadows neighborhood, positioned on a height of land that takes in panoramic ski run views," LaPay states.

Sources indicate that inside, the floors are French Vanilla slate from India. The great room opens to a south-facing deck that looks out at the runs of Park City Mountain Resort and Deer Valley Resort, each 10 to 15 minutes away.

Recent renovations reworked the kitchen and bathrooms. The kitchen now has gourmet appliances, custom cabinetry and an oversized island topped in marble, and the primary bathroom comes with an expansive steam shower. Other updates include a custom bunkroom, a gym and outdoor turf areas for recreation.

Outside, heated patios are linked by sculptural staircases, and the driveway is heated, too. A three-car garage completes the property.

"There is a wonderful walking path up to a summit that is perfect for a 'sundowner' gathering to enjoy sunsets," LaPay says.

The property borders Round Valley, a preserved open space with trails for hiking, biking and cross-country skiing that are maintained year-round.

Besides being close to the area's top ski resorts, the estate is less than 20 minutes from the historic Main Street and its shops, galleries and restaurants, and a five-minute drive from the Park Meadows Country Club.

Salt Lake City International Airport and private terminals in Salt Lake City and Heber City are all about 30 minutes away, close enough for a weekend of skiing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Thanksgiving marks the 100th anniversary of the annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, and while the weather forced the parade to be postponed for the first time in its history, thousands are still expected to cram the streets of Manhattan to watch the iconic event on its rescheduled date, Saturday.

But imagine having a front-row seat without ever leaving home?

There are plenty of apartments, condos, and penthouses that line the parade route that runs along Central Park, and we found four active listings that would allow you to watch the parade year after year without ever stepping outside.

Why it’s here: Residence 7C sits along Central Park West on West 75th Street, putting the parade right outside its windows.

“With over 45 feet of frontage along the parade route, balloons floating right past the windows, and sweeping southeast views, it's the ultimate vantage point for the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade,” explained listing agent Jessica Svensson of Douglas Elliman.

The 3,000-square-foot unit is distinguished by its grand prewar proportions, including a nearly 30-foot great room, a 21-foot formal dining room, and 10-foot ceilings.

Its gracious floor plan separates the entertaining spaces from the private bedroom wing, while the corner positioning offers sweeping views east across Central Park and south toward the Manhattan skyline and Billionaires' Row.

Other noteworthy features include a primary suite with western exposure, a flexible library or home office, an eat-in kitchen, central AC, a built-in bar with refrigeration, and a separate laundry room.

Jessica Svensson of Douglas Elliman is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: Thanks to the building’s 1931 column-free corner design, Units 5Q and 4P offer unobstructed northern views up Central Park West, ideal for watching the Thanksgiving Day Parade.

“For years three generations have gathered to watch the parade in this special home,” said listing agent Nealy Nusbaum Erber of Christie's International Real Estate New York.

The 3,000+ square foot apartment offers a truly magical sense of living among the treetops, with beautiful park views from all of the major entertaining rooms. The flexible floor initiative allows for a wonderful separation between the living and sleeping quarters, offering both gracious entertaining spaces and privacy.

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1347 w)

Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, just three of the 50 most populous U.S.
  • Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers.
  • Recent findings suggest that all three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

Recent findings suggest that all three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater Newly introduced York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

In a recent development, “Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” noted Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”.

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

Industry observers note that that marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

It has been revealed that when sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

Sources indicate that we estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan remarked. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a major hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate. With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”.

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

In a recent development, there were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

It has been revealed that on the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

According to recent reports, the number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more latest listings are adding to the major pool of supply.

According to recent reports, some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a upcoming job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

According to recent reports, for the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

Sources indicate that the Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

It has been revealed that house hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

According to recent reports, as a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends.   • eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

According to recent reports, brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the manufacturer.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, stated in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, indicates it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa stated in a statement.

In a recent development, rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the organization.

Industry observers note that jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen mentioned in a statement.

In a recent development, dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

Sources indicate that “Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs remarked in a statement.

Sources indicate that IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl mentioned in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the organization.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.
  • The AI selloff reportedly began in August.
  • Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:15 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Recent findings suggest that other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

According to recent reports, the semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

In a recent development, the stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The organization missed expectations across the board. Ambarella mentioned that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

Recent findings suggest that companies downstream from chipmakers in the AI data center supply chain fared better. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. ended the trading session 1.8% higher after dipping into the red earlier today, while Dell Technologies Inc. gained 0.64%.

In contrast, the major cloud providers weren’t left out of today’s selloff. Amazon.com Inc., the cloud market’s largest player, closed 3% lower. Microsoft Corp. and Google LLC dropped 1.25% and 2%, respectively. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an important AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

Anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The tech giant thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Sources indicate that overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

Breaking: Thanksgiving Murder Mystery Remains Unsolved 30 Years After Killer Allegedly Used Cat Door to Enter Woman’s Texas Apartment

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For 30 years, Thanksgiving has been a painful reminder for a Texas family whose holiday turned into a nightmare when their loved one was found strangled inside her Houston apartment.
  • Kristen Lea Wilson, 29, was preparing to spend Thanksgiving with her family in November 1996 when investigators say someone slipped into her first-floor apartment through a window, using a cat door to gain access, and waited for her to return home.
  • After cutting the telephone cord and unscrewing the lightbulbs to keep the apartment dark, the intruder waited in Wilson’s bedroom closet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 30 years, Thanksgiving has been a painful reminder for a Texas family whose holiday turned into a nightmare when their loved one was found strangled inside her Houston apartment.

Kristen Lea Wilson, 29, was preparing to spend Thanksgiving with her family in November 1996 when investigators say someone slipped into her first-floor apartment through a window, using a cat door to gain access, and waited for her to return home.

After cutting the telephone cord and unscrewing the lightbulbs to keep the apartment dark, the intruder waited in Wilson’s bedroom closet.

When she never highlighted up to Thanksgiving dinner the following day, her parents became worried and drove her apartment where they found her slain body. Three decades later, no one has been charged in her murder, and her family is still fighting for answers.

According to recent reports, “Thirty years ago this Thanksgiving my sister Kristen Lea Wilson was murdered in Houston,” Kelly Wilson Hancock wrote in a recent social media post. “She was strangled–this was an up and personal murder. Her case has NEVER been solved.”.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 27, 1996, the day before Thanksgiving, Wilson stopped at a grocery store after work to pick up last-minute items for the family's holiday gathering at her grandparents' home in Katy, TX.

In a recent development, she returned to her apartment on Meadowglen Lane in southwest Houston, unloaded her groceries, and reportedly went into her bedroom to change clothes. Investigators believe her killer was already inside.

It has been revealed that according to the Houston Police Department, the intruder likely gained access by reaching through a cat door in the screen of a first-floor window and removing the window frame. Once inside, the killer allegedly cut the telephone cord and unscrewed lightbulbs, reportedly preparing to ambush Wilson in complete darkness.

Industry observers note that the apartment's accessibility became a crucial detail in the investigation, and raised troubling questions about security at the complex, especially because Wilson had allegedly expressed concerns about her safety before her death, her family stated. She had previously revealed an incident in which a maintenance worker allegedly entered her apartment without warning.

According to recent reports, when Wilson’s parents arrived at her apartment to check on her, they found the front door unlocked. Inside, Wilson's father made the horrific discovery–his daughter dead on the bedroom floor. She had been strangled and was partially undressed.

Police also noted a disturbing detail–her body appeared to have been deliberately positioned, with her ankles crossed and her hands resting in her lap.

Investigators found evidence of a violent struggle, including broken fingernails, suggesting Wilson had fought desperately against her attacker. There were no reported witnesses to the killing, and surveillance cameras did not capture the suspect leaving the property.

Despite decades of investigation, extensive media coverage and advancements in forensic technologies, the identity of Wilson’s killer remains a mystery.

Three men associated with Wilson provided DNA samples to investigators shortly after her death, and each were ruled out as suspects based on the technology available at the time, according to an investigation by ABC13 Houston.

But Hancock believes mistakes made during the initial investigation have complicated efforts to solve her sister's murder.

“From the get go, the detectives messed up,” she wrote in her recent post. “The original detective was going through a divorce and she wasn’t focused.”.

Sources indicate that she also expressed frustration over what she described as inconsistencies in the investigation. Investigators have since discovered that not all the evidence collected from the crime scene was tested, according to local reports.

Hancock mentioned she has attempted to contact Othram, a forensic DNA laboratory that specializes in helping law enforcement investigate cold cases, about potentially examining evidence in her sister's murder.

“I’ve tried to reach out to Othram Labs to see if they can look at DNA, but the detective has to request it, from what I am told,” she wrote.

It is unclear whether Houston police have submitted evidence for additional testing or whether forensic genetic genealogy could be used in the case.

For the Wilson family, Thanksgiving had always been one of their favorite celebrations.

Industry observers note that “Thanksgiving was the biggest event of the year,” Hancock told ABC13. “We’d all go over there, and it was just a significant family get-together. It was so much fun.”.

Wilson, described by her sister as independent and ambitious, had debuted a small business that provided office services to local companies. Wilson, the middle of three girls, was also devoted to her family, especially her young niece and nephew.

Industry observers note that "She was like a second mother to my son and daughter,” Hancock remarked. “She was just so beautiful with an infectious smile. My mom always called her the golden child because she just was. I hate to say she was perfect, but she pretty much was.”.

The Wilson family was devastated by her murder and to this day are still struggling with questions that remain unanswered three decades later.

“My grandma used the words ‘brutally murdered.’ I’ll never forget the call telling me Kristen had been killed," Hancock noted. "My whole world was… our whole family’s world was turned upside down. Personally, I think she knew the person, but I don’t know.".

Wilson's father, who discovered her body, has since passed away without learning who killed his daughter.

As the family marks the 30th anniversary of Wilson's death this Thanksgiving, her sister continues to push for answers.

Recent findings suggest that hancock mentioned Houston police Detective Richard Rodriguez, who previously discussed the case in ABC13's Unsolved series, is now handling the investigation. When John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house.

Sources indicate that joseph P. Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat.

It has been revealed that five years earlier, it was what happened after Thanksgiving dinner that the family would remember. John, then a Massachusetts senator, slipped into the study off the living room with his father.

Recent findings suggest that he had a list of reasons to think twice about running for president. Joseph had an answer for every one.

By the time they emerged, the Kennedys had a campaign to initiative.

Industry observers note that the house where that conversation took place began as a summer rental. In 1926, Joseph and his wife, Rose, brought their children to Malcolm Cottage, a waterfront home overlooking Nantucket Sound. John was just 9.

According to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum, Joseph bought the property two years later for $25,000 and expanded the house to accommodate his growing family.

John eventually bought a place of his own behind his parents’ home. His brother Robert and sister-in-law Ethel came to own an adjoining property.

Together, the three residences formed the 6-acre compound, an arrangement that put several generations of Kennedys within walking distance of Thanksgiving dinner at the Substantial House.

Industry observers note that in "White House by the Sea," author Kate Storey describes a family with surprisingly little use for a formal seating proposal. Joseph and Rose took opposite ends of the mahogany table.

Industry observers note that everyone else picked a spot. Family cook Ziptha Anderson remembered far less flexibility when it came to carving the bird.

“They all like the same thing—the white meat,” she mentioned.

According to recent reports, the weather had a say in the menu, too. A chilly Thanksgiving called for clam broth, while a mild afternoon meant tomato juice to start.

It has been revealed that dinner was at 1 p.m. in Storey’s account of the 1956 gathering, which still left the family time for Mass and a sail before they made their way to the table.

In a recent development, by Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay, then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children.

Recent findings suggest that one family outing took the president and several of his siblings to the skating rink in Hyannis named for their late brother, Joseph Jr. John watched while Ted and his sisters rented skates and played tag on the ice.

According to recent reports, back at the compound, Bobby and Ted also got a touch football game going. That evening, the adults sat down to Vermont turkey, candied sweet potatoes, and their choice of pies.

Recent findings suggest that ted found another way to work up an appetite in 1979. A United Press International photographer caught the senator waving from his boat as he took relatives and friends sailing off Hyannis Port before Thanksgiving dinner.

Ethel carried on hosting Thanksgiving at Hyannis Port long after her children had families of their own. In 2010, she enlisted her son Robert to bring home two live turkeys so her grandchildren could see the birds up close. One promptly escaped.

“For three days they chased it everywhere,” Ethel told the Cape Cod Times.

A couple of months later, the newspaper ran a story about a turkey causing trouble in nearby Centerville, where it had even taken on a moving postal truck. Ethel called the newsroom. She thought she knew where the bird had come from.

#225407. Tech Report: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2201 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Redfin ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • Industry observers note that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Industry observers note that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

Sources indicate that this is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

It has been revealed that two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

Industry observers note that “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

Industry observers note that millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

In a recent development, adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

It has been revealed that baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

In a recent development, but their housing burden fell promptly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

In a recent development, millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

Industry observers note that “The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao mentioned. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

Industry observers note that that dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

Recent findings suggest that the same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

It has been revealed that consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Sources indicate that home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Industry observers note that monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

Sources indicate that income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

It has been revealed that how to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report demonstrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

#225406. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (963 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople.
  • I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since.
  • In a recent development, you didn’t fail the program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

In a recent development, you didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

Sources indicate that the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

It has been revealed that this isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

Recent findings suggest that the veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

It has been revealed that we do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

Recent findings suggest that what would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

Recent findings suggest that there’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

Sources indicate that we haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

It has been revealed that we’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

In a recent development, you aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

According to recent reports, lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Identity security tech giant 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.
  • In a recent development, according to the firm, the incident came to light on Nov.
  • The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:29 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Identity security tech giant 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

In a recent development, according to the firm, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is noted to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”.

The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company indicates, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Beyond the customer records, the attacker is noted to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the organization claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

According to recent reports, the tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. People with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, stated to be a small number, have been notified directly.

In a recent development, as a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password notes it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning users to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

According to recent reports, this is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the firm said that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will enhancement its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995.
  • Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A co-living community in West Oakland, CA, has hit the market for the first time.

Industry observers note that the Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995. That’s the asking price for all three homes. If purchased separately by friends, multigenerational families, or any other buyers who want to live side by side, the starting price is $899,000 for the smallest of the three homes, which has five bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound.

This lot has been zoned RM-3, or Mixed Housing Type Residential–3, which allows for multiple single-family homes on a single lot. This setup is permissible due to changes in California law allowing for higher-density housing in residential areas.

This project started in 2019 when a startup called Open Door bought the 7,535-square-foot empty lot and tasked Matt Baran of Baran Studio Architecture with creating a co-living space.

They asked: “What if we design something that can be beautiful design and work with the fresh state laws that allow for increased density in neighborhoods and works well for community living?” claims listing agent Max Nelson, who specializes in co-living sales through the platform Live Near Friends.

The end result was a rent-by-the-room community where residents enjoyed shared amenities, including a backyard fire pit, co-working space, and rooftop deck with views of downtown Oakland.

The design process balanced group-friendly amenities with the look and feel of the neighborhood, which is filled with mostly Victorian homes.

Nelson claims that the architects asked, “How do we create a modern house without making it look like it doesn't fit?”.

Recent findings suggest that the design included bay windows that jut from the homes, mirroring the style of a classic Victorian. Having three separate homes rather than one huge building also matched the aesthetic of the area, as did the incorporation of tall, narrow windows.

Sources indicate that much of the rest of the design leans more modern, especially the efficient energy systems. The homes rely on shared solar panels, greatly reducing energy bills. Everything is electric—there is no reliance on gas. Each room has its own fan coils to create customized comfort.

“It’s a super efficient, well-done system,” says Nelson.

Because The Union was designed for co-living, some of the best features are the shared spaces and the flow among the three homes.

The property fronting the street, 1514, has the smaller price tag at $899,000 and offers 1,919 square feet of living space, including five bedrooms and four bathrooms. A skybridge connects it with the back two condos, positioned side by side like a duplex and sharing a common wall.

Industry observers note that the larger of the back condos, 1510, is listed at $1,049,500 and sits slightly larger at 2,033 square feet, again with five bedrooms and four bathrooms. Connected is 1512, also offered at $1,049,500 with 2,015 square feet, including four bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Above these two condos is the roof area, which houses the solar panels as well as the communal deck with AstroTurf and several seating areas.

It all adds up to a highly functional, thoughtfully designed compound that meets the needs of communal living. It offers both shared spaces as well as smaller decks, outdoor seating nooks, and private spaces for solo or one-on-one time with another—because shared living works best when people have the freedom to come together or enjoy time apart.
