Industry News: Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.
  • Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules.
  • The company revealed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company revealed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

In a recent development, the announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

Recent findings suggest that “Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson mentioned in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”.

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the manufacturer.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson mentioned.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The fresh complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

According to recent reports, on Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the problem in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services.

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Recent findings suggest that amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS declared aims for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton noted the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

Industry observers note that the growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

According to recent reports, compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.

Upcoming release helps users organize project context, carry it between computers, and choose exactly what their models receive.

According to recent reports, FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Intersignal LLC today unveiled Braid 2.2, an update to its free local AI workspace that introduces named memory containers, reviewed memory bundles, searchable project context, and visible context budgets.

According to recent reports, braid connects local model conversations with project Channels, approved rig connections, an agent review Inbox, and built-in Folio publishing. Version 2.2 gives users a more organized way to preserve the mission, decisions, constraints, and next steps they want available in future conversations.

In a recent development, "Running a model on your own hardware is a powerful starting point. Keeping a project moving across conversations and computers is the next practical challenge," said David Seaman, founder of Intersignal. "Braid 2.2 lets people decide what is worth keeping, carry it between rigs, and inspect exactly what context their model was given.".

Recent findings suggest that give Each Mission a HomeMemory containers group related capsules within a Channel. Each capsule contains five editable fields: title, mission, decisions, constraints, and next steps.

Recent findings suggest that customers can search capsule text, filter by container, and inspect the exact size of their selected memory context. A Channel can include up to four capsules within a 12,000-byte serialized context budget.

Industry observers note that saving memory and including it in chat remain separate choices. New and imported capsules start excluded. Users select the capsules they want, enable the Channel's context permission, and choose whether to include that context in a chat request. Editing or moving a capsule clears its inclusion so the changed revision can be reviewed again.

Carry Reviewed Context Between RigsA complete container can be exported as a readable file and imported into another Channel or rig. The destination presents the container and every capsule's exact fields for review before confirmation.Confirmed imports receive newly introduced local identities and start excluded from chat. Existing individual memory capsule files remain supported.

Memory files carry selected project context. They do not automatically synchronize computers, publish conversations, or grant permissions to connected AI clients. Chat receipts show the exact capsule revisions supplied to a model.

More Care for Work in ProgressBraid 2.2 also preserves unsent chat drafts when users switch Channels within the same open window, asks before discarding changed memory fields, and saves capsule text and container changes together. Additional fixes guard against delayed responses changing the active conversation.

The release retains Braid's now familiar chat interface and text effect, reviewed agent proposals, approved rig handoffs, and Folio's workflow for shaping selected material into a public edition.

Sources indicate that availabilityBraid 2.2 is available at https://intersignal.org/.Users configure their model server and weights separately. Braid supports Ollama and local or LAN OpenAI-compatible inference endpoints, including servers provided by tools such as vLLM and LM Studio.

About IntersignalIntersignal LLC builds software for local AI, deliberate context sharing, and publishing under human control. Its Braid workspace brings local model conversations, project memory, rig connections, agent review, and Folio publishing into one application.

Artificial intelligence developer ElevenLabs Inc. is reportedly in early talks to raise capital at a $33 billion valuation.

Bloomberg today cited sources as saying that the manufacturer plans to close the round in the first quarter of 2027. According to the report, some investors are pushing for the raise to happen sooner. Industry observers note that it’s unclear how much ElevenLabs hopes to raise or from whom. Late-stage startup investments almost always include contributions from existing backers. ElevenLabs’ most recent raise, which valued it at $22 billion, saw the participation of Nvidia Corp.’s NVentures fund, Blackrock, Wellington and several others.

In a recent development, elevenLabs’ fundraising push reportedly comes amid a surge in customer demand. Its annualized revenue is said to have grown by $100 million since September, to $700 million.

It has been revealed that founded in 2022, ElevenLabs develops a series of AI models optimized to process audio. Companies use them to field call center inquiries, transcribe meetings, generate music and perform related tasks. It also offers a service called Productions that delivers ready-to-use audio assets.

The tech giant debuted its newest and most capable model, Eleven v4, in late September. The algorithm’s flagship feature is its ability to tailor its speaking style to each text snippet. It does so by automatically tuning parameters such as tone and pacing.

Consumers can manually customize Eleven v4’s speaking style by adding instructions to scripts. They can also generate conversations with multiple synthetic speakers. A real-time version of the model, Eleven v4 Turbo, generates audio with only 150 milliseconds of latency for use cases such as customer support.

ElevenLabs offers Eleven v4 alongside more narrowly focused models. In May, it introduced an algorithm specifically optimized to dub videos. Additionally, it provides developer tools that make it easier to integrate its AI models into enterprise applications.

It’s possible ElevenLabs is raising upcoming capital to finance more acquisitions. Earlier this month, it agreed to buy Kotoba Inc., a startup that develops audio processing models for companies in Japan. Nikkei Asia reported that the deal is worth $100 million. ElevenLabs will hire more salespeople in Japan over the next few months to grow its market presence.

A few days before the acquisition, ElevenLabs chief executive Mati Staniszewski stated that the company intends to start preparing for an initial public offering in 2028. That time frame suggests the round the software maker is right now raising could be followed by additional venture investments.

Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.
  • I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.
  • We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to blueprint. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

It has been revealed that we recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

According to recent reports, we eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

In a recent development, I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein).

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

In a recent development, this has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

According to recent reports, I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

In a recent development, once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

In a recent development, what I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:.

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”.

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

How State Environmental Laws Are Being ‘Weaponized’ To Stall Housing and Drive Up Costs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.
  • The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing.
  • According to recent reports, the study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.

The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing. This comes as state lawmakers have proposed many upcoming laws this year to curtail policies that stall building, with mixed success.

According to recent reports, the study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws. Both of these kinds of disputes are expensive and time-consuming. Developers have to examine and reexamine the environmental impact of developments they want to build, and courts must then determine what cities are required to do to ensure a clean environment for residents.

"A real cost is borne on the people who are renting and buying those homes and apartments," Kyle Sweetland, the study's author, tells Realtor.com®.

Recent findings suggest that about a dozen states have pitched laws that would make it easier to build homes, many of them by reducing zoning or lot size requirements. But some proposals have also met with failure, like California's Proposition 45, which aimed to expedite project reviews through the California Environmental Quality Act.

Industry observers note that the Realtor.com Housing Supply Gap research shows the U.S. faces a shortage of 4.03 million homes. Our Let America Build campaign has tracked how states have responded to this shortage, and which are tackling the problem.

California has a long history of slow development on account of environmental review. In one recent example, a 49-unit housing development was stalled for 4.5 years in environmental litigation, which the developer said had raised the cost of the project by $9 million. In another, a 34-home subdivision was stalled for nearly 40 years, in part because of neighbors' environmental concerns.

In a recent development, it's not just a California problem. Sweetland looked at 16 states and the District of Columbia that have environmental policy acts that affect developers, or amendments that affect municipalities. Wyoming, Minnesota, New York, Hawaii, and Massachusetts have both.

But other protections are also in place in California, Nevada, Washington, North Dakota, Illinois, Wyoming, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Upcoming Jersey, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia.

Sources indicate that it's hard to track precisely how much this kind of litigation drives up the costs of housing. Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner also notes that it's hard to tell how many housing projects didn't start in the first place because developers expected a lawsuit.

In a recent development, "The bigger costs come from what the lawsuit does to the project’s financing and schedule," Berner says. "Appeals typically add years, and in the meantime, most projects can’t secure construction or grant funding. Loans, taxes, and insurance keep accruing, and construction costs can rise while the project waits.".

Change could come at the federal level. Last week, the Senate passed a controversial bill that would reduce some federal environmental regulations, like the National Environmental Policy Act, to speed up construction of big-energy projects. Environmental groups opposed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which next heads to the House.

According to recent reports, in some instances, the environmental lawsuits don't actually produce better outcomes for the environment. Seattle found that just 16% of cases filed using environmental laws over the 2010s resulted in decisions requiring environmental remediation. In Latest York, about 22% of cases over 15 years resulted in more environmental reviews, an outside researcher found.

Industry observers note that berner says the balance is that environmental laws are sometimes the easiest avenue residents have to oppose a residential project. It's just a matter of not abusing the process.

Sources indicate that "While challenging a project is a relatively cheap thing to do, being on the receiving end of a legal battle can derail a project even without going all the way through the litigation process," Berner claims. "This uncertainty adds to the cost of capital for builders and squeezes out lower-margin projects like affordable and infill housing.".

Sources indicate that pacific Legal Foundation states one solution for these issues is to narrow the scope of some environmental laws. For instance, Sweetland says legal challenges from outside environmental groups could be limited. That way, the people challenging housing developments have a real vested interest in their outcomes.

Industry observers note that he also suggests requirements that groups that lose cases have to pay the legal fees. That isn't typical everywhere, even if developers pay the legal fees when they lose. That provides some incentive that those launching lawsuits have a legitimate claim, as opposed to using the courts as a stalling tactic.

"The law shouldn't just give anybody the ability to have a license to stop a building from moving forward," Sweetland claims.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

In a recent development, DENVILLE, N.J., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What should first-time buyers evaluate before purchasing a certified pre-owned luxury vehicle?

HelloNation has published an article featuring insights from Steve Lustig of Autosport Acura of Denville, explaining how certified pre-owned luxury vehicles may offer a practical balance between premium features and manageable long-term ownership costs.

The article explains that many first-time buyers consider certified pre-owned luxury vehicles because they often provide advanced technology, premium interior materials, and modern safety systems at a lower purchase price than brand-fresh models. According to the article, understanding how manufacturer certification programs work may help buyers feel more confident throughout the purchasing process and future luxury vehicle ownership experience.

Industry observers note that one of the largest advantages discussed throughout the article is the inspection process required for certified pre-owned luxury vehicles. Many manufacturer programs require detailed multi-point inspections that evaluate major mechanical systems, electronics, brakes, tires, suspension components, and safety features before certification is approved. These inspections may help buyers feel more comfortable regarding vehicle reliability and overall condition.

Sources indicate that warranty coverage is another major topic highlighted in the article. Manufacturer-backed warranty coverage may provide protection for certain repairs and mechanical concerns after purchase. Compared to standard used vehicles without certification, certified pre-owned luxury vehicles often include more structured warranty coverage designed to reduce unexpected repair expenses during the ownership period. The article explains that carefully reviewing warranty coverage terms, duration, and limitations is an important step before making a purchase decision.

It has been revealed that the HelloNation article also discusses the value of roadside assistance programs that are frequently included with manufacturer certification packages. Services such as towing support, flat tire assistance, battery service, and emergency roadside assistance may provide additional confidence for individuals entering luxury vehicle ownership for the first time. According to the article, roadside assistance programs often add value beyond the vehicle itself while helping drivers feel more prepared for unexpected situations.

Vehicle history reports are another crucial factor addressed throughout the article. Buyers are encouraged to review vehicle history reports carefully before purchasing certified pre-owned luxury vehicles. Accident history, previous ownership records, title status, and service information may all influence long-term reliability and resale value. Even when certification inspections have been completed, vehicle history reports remain an important tool for evaluating the overall condition and ownership background of a vehicle.

Maintenance records are also discussed as a key consideration for first-time buyers. Luxury vehicles often include specialized engineering and advanced performance systems that benefit from consistent service according to manufacturer recommendations. Reviewing maintenance records may help buyers confirm whether oil changes, brake service, tire maintenance, and other scheduled services were completed properly over time. Certified pre-owned luxury vehicles with strong maintenance records may provide greater confidence regarding long-term reliability.

The article further explains that technology features continue to attract many buyers to certified pre-owned luxury vehicles. Modern luxury vehicles often include premium sound systems, advanced infotainment platforms, driver assistance technology, navigation systems, and upgraded safety features. Purchasing certified pre-owned models may allow drivers to access these premium technologies at a more manageable overall cost.

Long-term ownership costs are another vital consideration discussed throughout the article. While certified models may reduce initial purchase expenses compared to new vehicles, buyers should still evaluate insurance costs, future maintenance expectations, tire replacement expenses, and potential repair needs. Understanding warranty coverage, maintenance records, and manufacturer certification standards may help buyers make more informed luxury vehicle ownership decisions.

The article concludes that carefully reviewing inspection standards, vehicle history reports, roadside assistance programs, maintenance records, and warranty coverage may help first-time buyers better understand the long-term value of certified pre-owned luxury vehicles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that while it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he mentioned.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

In a recent development, sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A significant part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively newly introduced sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move promptly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

According to recent reports, what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré mentioned. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

Sources indicate that but that can be a long road. Sangaré mentioned it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

It has been revealed that and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

LINCOLN, Neb., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Amore Italy (AmoreItaly.com), a Nebraska based, luxury travel organization specializing in all-inclusive, private-driver tours of Italy, today announced significant enhancements to its 2027 travel program, including complimentary luxury villa upgrades valued at $12,000, expanded itineraries, and a Black Friday promotion offering free airfare up to $1,000 per person.

The announcement follows an exceptionally successful inaugural 2026 season, during which September and October tours completely sold out, leaving no additional availability during the popular autumn travel season. "We could not be more pleased with the success of our first season," noted Steve Glenn, President of Amore Italy. "Travelers are looking for something dramatically different from traditional motorcoach tours. They want the luxury of a private driver, the intimacy of traveling with friends and family, and an authentic Italian experience where virtually every detail is taken care of.".

Black Friday Special: FREE Airfare Up to $1,000 Per Person*.

To celebrate its expanded 2027 program, Amore Italy is launching a limited-time Black Friday promotion. Travelers reserving 2027 Amore Italy tours between November 27 and December 4, 2026, will receive an airfare benefit of up to $1,000 per person. "With the tremendous demand we experienced this fall, we want to give travelers an extraordinary incentive to reserve their 2027 Italian vacation early," mentioned Glenn.

Complimentary $12,000 Luxury Villa Upgrade.

One of the most exciting enhancements for 2027 is the opportunity for private groups of six to eight travelers to enjoy a complimentary six-night upgrade to Villa Destino, a magnificent six-bedroom luxury villa in the medieval Umbrian village of Montone. For eligible departures between May and October 2027, groups may upgrade from the 4-Star Hotel Fortebraccio & Spa to Villa Destino, subject to availability. The upgrade represents approximately $12,000 in accommodation value at no additional cost.

A Different Way to Experience Italy.

Amore Italy's signature experiences include private transportation, luxury accommodations, authentic Italian cooking classes, visits to medieval villages, exceptional dining, local wines, and its celebrated grand lunch and wine tasting at Cantina Blasi in Umbria. "Our guests aren't simply purchasing a vacation," Glenn concluded. "They are investing in memories they will cherish for the rest of their lives. We believe the future of luxury travel is about meaningful experiences, exceptional service, and making every moment count.".

2027 Reservations Now Available.

Reservations for Amore Italy's 2027 private-driver tours are now open. The Black Friday airfare promotion is available for 2027 reservations made November 27 through December 4, 2026.

#225366. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that want to price more precisely?
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Sources indicate that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

According to recent reports, A sold comp tells us where a buyer noted yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Industry observers note that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

According to recent reports, one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

Recent findings suggest that it also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Recent findings suggest that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Industry observers note that listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

It has been revealed that find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

Recent findings suggest that we’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • It has been revealed that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

It has been revealed that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

It has been revealed that “Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont remarked in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon mentioned in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Recent findings suggest that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan mentioned in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an notable step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

In a recent development, inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel remarked. “I think it’s key to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

According to recent reports, tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

Sources indicate that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KeyBank shares warning signs and practical steps for avoiding phishing, fake shopping sites, payment app scams and other holiday fraud.

In a recent development, CLEVELAND, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As holiday shopping picks up, so do opportunities for scammers.

Consumers shopping online, tracking packages, buying gift cards or donating to charities can encounter increasingly convincing fraud attempts. Scammers are also using artificial intelligence to create fake retail websites, emails, text messages and even AI-generated voices designed to impersonate trusted companies or people.

Knowing what to look for can help consumers recognize potential fraud before they share personal information or send money.

What are the most common holiday shopping scams?

Here are several scams consumers should watch for during the holiday season:.

Bank imposter scams. Fraudsters may call, text or email pretending to represent a consumer's bank. They may claim there has been a suspicious transaction or login attempt, then ask for a one-time passcode, login credentials or debit card information. KeyBank will not initiate a call or text asking for your online banking username or password. KeyBank also will not ask a client to send money to themselves using ZelleÂ®, an account transfer or a wire payment, or request remote access to your computer or mobile device. However, in some cases, we will call to verify your identity by asking for a one-time passcode that is sent to your mobile device.

Phishing and smishing scams. Fraudulent emails and text messages can look like legitimate communications from retailers, banks or delivery companies. Scammers may also use AI to create convincing fake retail websites and communications intended to capture debit card, credit card or other personal information. A common example is a fake package-delivery message asking for payment to release or redeliver an order.

It has been revealed that vishing and AI voice scams. Criminals can use AI-generated voices in phone calls to impersonate customer service representatives, delivery companies, family members or others in an effort to obtain sensitive information.

Recent findings suggest that payment app scams. Consumers should be cautious when an unfamiliar seller asks for payment through ZelleÂ®, Venmo, Cash App, wire transfer or cryptocurrency. Recovering money sent to a fraudulent seller through these methods can be difficult.

Recent findings suggest that online marketplace scams. Fraudsters may advertise popular holiday gifts at unusually low prices, then request advance payment through a payment app, gift card or cryptocurrency before disappearing.

Gift card scams. Criminals may tamper with gift cards displayed on retail racks or convince victims to provide gift card numbers over the phone to make supposedly urgent payments.

Charity scams. The season of giving can also attract criminals impersonating legitimate charities or disaster-relief organizations through phone calls, texts, emails and social media.

What should you do if you think you've been scammed?

Consumers who believe they have been targeted or have already sent money should contact their financial institution immediately and report suspected fraud to the retailer and appropriate authorities. KeyBank clients can contact the KeyBank Fraud Client Service Center at 1-800-433-0124. Dial 711 for TTY/TRS.

Additional information about emerging scams, account security and fraud prevention is available at key.com/fraud.

Ultimately, one of the strongest defenses against holiday fraud is taking a moment before responding. An unexpected message, urgent request or unusually attractive deal is worth verifying independently before clicking a link, providing information or sending money.

#225359. Industry News: Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (852 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?
  • Industry observers note that identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:52 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

Industry observers note that identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

In a recent development, artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

Recent findings suggest that agentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

Language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

Permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

AgentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more important point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

The companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. According to recent reports, SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mediwhale, an AI healthcare company that uses noninvasive retinal imaging to assess the risk of cardiometabolic diseases, today announced that it has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for Dr. Noon CVD, its retinal-AI cardiovascular risk assessment software. The clearance paves the way for Mediwhale to introduce Dr. Noon CVD into U.S. clinical practice.

In a recent development, dr. Noon CVD combines AI analysis of retinal images with age and sex to estimate an individual's 10-year risk of a first atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Results classify patients into one of three risk categories to support clinicians' cardiovascular risk assessment alongside other clinical information.[1].

Cardiovascular prevention in the United States is placing greater emphasis on earlier intervention informed by individualized risk assessment, as reflected in the 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline on the management of dyslipidemia.[2] Mediwhale aims to contribute to this approach by offering clinicians a noninvasive way to assess cardiovascular risk through retinal imaging.

In a recent development, "Retinal cameras are already in primary care clinics across the United States, where they are used every day for diabetic eye exams," remarked Kevin Taegeun Choi, CEO of Mediwhale. "With FDA clearance, that same retinal exam can now do more: support cardiovascular risk assessment. We intend to be first to bring this to U.S. primary care, working with partners that already operate these networks and building U.S. real-world data as we go.".

Sources indicate that mediwhale is an AI healthcare organization that uses noninvasive retinal imaging to assess cardiometabolic disease risk. In the United States, Dr. Noon CVD is FDA-cleared software for cardiovascular risk assessment. For more information, visit https://mediwhale.com/.

  • The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates remarked, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

It has been revealed that she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Newly introduced America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

According to recent reports, sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers mentioned they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

Industry observers note that “Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

Sources indicate that she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

It has been revealed that in its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

#225352. Why biodiversity belongs in the master proposal

Why biodiversity belongs in the master proposal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking.
  • Recent findings suggest that parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment.
  • Pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that master-planned communities have always been exercises in long-term thinking. Decisions about infrastructure, open space, water, landscaping and mobility made early in the planning process shape how a community functions decades later.

Recent findings suggest that parks, drainage areas and open spaces require substantial investment. But there’s growing evidence that designing those landscapes to support biodiversity can help that investment do more. Planned early as part of the infrastructure conversation, biodiversity can help a community better manage water, withstand environmental stress and create stronger connections between residents and the natural environment.

Pollinator habitats offer one of the most practical places to begin. Bees, butterflies and other pollinators help many flowering plants reproduce, sustaining vegetation that supports broader ecosystems.

In a recent development, development decisions can remove or fragment the food sources and nesting areas those species need. At the scale of a master-planned community, developers have an opportunity to connect habitat across parks, drainage corridors and neighborhoods, making conservation part of the places people use every day.

Sources indicate that developers already expect infrastructure to serve a defined purpose and perform over time. Landscape systems deserve the same scrutiny.

A stormwater basin can manage runoff while also providing habitat. A trail corridor can connect residents to destinations while connecting pollinators to food and nesting resources. Plant selection can account for seasonal habitat needs alongside appearance and maintenance.

Recent findings suggest that these decisions are much more than aesthetic considerations. A 2024 npj Urban Sustainability review examining research across stormwater management, water purification, heat mitigation, infrastructure resilience and maintenance costs found that biodiversity can meaningfully influence how blue-green infrastructure performs. More diverse ecological systems were associated with benefits ranging from improved stormwater retention and water purification to greater resilience under changing environmental conditions.

Industry observers note that for developers, the implication is practical: Ecological and engineering performance do not necessarily need to be treated as separate objectives. Incorporating habitat into drainage or open-space aims creates opportunities to serve multiple purposes within the same land area. It also brings stewardship into the budget early, when responsibilities can be assigned, and maintenance requirements can inform design.

In a recent development, the value of parks, trails and public spaces extends beyond a direct line-item return. Planning those landscapes to support biodiversity adds another dimension to that investment, allowing them to contribute to ecological health while serving the needs of the community.

Sources indicate that pollinators depend on more than a patch of flowers. They need plants that provide resources throughout the growing season, places to nest and landscapes they can move through. An isolated garden may offer some of those resources, but a coordinated network can support them across a larger area.

Research highlights how much landscape design can matter. A 2026 study published in Urban Ecosystems compared two newly developed residential neighborhoods and found that pollinator abundance and diversity were two to three times higher in the neighborhood dominated by native plants than in one with conventional landscaping. Despite similar numbers of flowers, the difference suggests that what developers plant can matter as much as how much they plant.

According to recent reports, master-planned communities have an unusual ability to create that network. Developers overseeing hundreds or thousands of acres can coordinate planting and habitat connections across property lines and development phases.

Rather than treating pollinator-friendly landscaping as a one-time intervention, the strategy needs to evolve alongside the community. Establishing baseline ecological conditions before construction and continuing monitoring as development progresses creates a reference point to evaluate changes over time.

In a recent development, that approach also requires considering habitat connectivity throughout the development process. Native plantings, open spaces and landscape corridors can be incorporated into the broader plan, rather than treated as isolated conservation features.

As developers, we routinely track home sales, water use, construction costs and other indicators of a community’s performance. Tracking ecological outcomes brings that same discipline to landscape investments.

At Baseline, a 1,100-acre master-planned community in Broomfield, Colorado, Butterfly Pavilion introduced its Pollinator District model in 2019, integrating conservation into development and ongoing operations. With monitoring in place before construction, researchers recorded 3,805 macropollinators in developed areas in 2025, up from 587 in 2023, an increase of more than 500%.

Recent findings suggest that but numbers alone don’t tell the full story. Much of the increase came from nonnative western honeybees, making pollinator diversity an equally vital measure of progress. The findings also highlight opportunities for additional native plantings to better support native bees.

The broader lesson is that ecological performance can be measured, and those findings can inform future decisions. Pollinator counts alone cannot establish the impact of every landscape intervention, but monitoring provides a way to identify changes, evaluate habitat strategies and adjust as development progresses.

That same principle can apply beyond pollinators. Whether evaluating stormwater systems, native landscaping or habitat corridors, establishing meaningful measures of performance can help developers better understand the long-term outcomes of their investments.

Industry observers note that integrating biodiversity also creates an ongoing opportunity to learn. Working with ecological specialists helps developers understand the starting landscape, set meaningful goals and see how it responds. That work needs to carry into everyday landscape care, from what gets planted to how areas are mowed and pests are managed, with resources and responsibility for stewardship established for the years ahead.

Monitoring can guide future plant selections and help identify gaps in habitat connections as new neighborhoods take shape. It also requires consistency and an understanding that ecological conditions vary with weather, seasonal timing and other factors.

Protected lands and conservation areas remain essential to ecological health, but developed communities can contribute, too. Places designed for people can also provide meaningful habitat when ecological considerations are incorporated into planning and long-term operations.

It has been revealed that for developers, this is part of the longer commitment that comes with creating a master-planned community. These are places people will call home for decades, and caring for their ecological health is another part of planning for how they perform and evolve over that same horizon.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, declared the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Sources indicate that howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Industry observers note that people cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Recent findings suggest that howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it debuted publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

According to recent reports, the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of customers. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.
