Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • It has been revealed that the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

It has been revealed that the bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

According to recent reports, testing that more closely replicates the tech giant’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company claims it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software enhancement that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July enhancement was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report indicates.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

According to recent reports, third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report states.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate matter.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft claims it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also intends to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

In a recent development, some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

In a recent development, microsoft indicates its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft stated the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it indicates. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

The latest testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the firm states, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

Sources indicate that are Ripple’s XRP, Cardano (ADA), and Polygon (POL) losing their appeal among crypto investors in 2026? Ben Simpson, founder of crypto investment platform Collective Shift, has named all three among six altcoins he claims he wouldn’t touch with a 10-foot pole, citing concerns ranging from weak network activity and questionable valuations to intensifying competition. His blunt assessment raises fresh questions about which altcoins have the strongest fundamentals to survive the increasingly competitive crypto market.

In his post on X, Simpson acknowledged XRP’s role in enabling near-instant, inexpensive payments on the XRP Ledger but argued that the token lacks a compelling mechanism for capturing the value generated by Ripple’s business growth.

Recent findings suggest that XRP enables fast, low-cost payments on the XRP Ledger.My issue with XRP is it's "value capture".When a business grows, I want to see how that success benefits the token I'm holding. In this case, there is none. Ripple can grow its revenue, but holders don't receive those….

His main concern is that Ripple’s commercial success does not necessarily translate into direct financial benefits for XRP holders. Even as the San Francisco-headquartered organization expands its revenue and boosts its payment operations, investors do not receive a share of those profits.

He also pointed out that Ripple does not use its business earnings to buy back XRP, a mechanism that could potentially create additional demand for the token. For Simpson, the absence of both profit-sharing and a buyback program makes it difficult to establish a direct link between Ripple’s growing business and XRP’s price in the long term.

He considers these shortcomings significant enough to keep XRP off his investment list, despite the network’s payment capabilities.

Sources indicate that simpson also expressed reservations about Cardano, arguing that its adoption level does not justify its market valuation. Although ADA powers a blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications, he believes the network is generating relatively little economic activity compared with its overall market size.

To support his argument, Simpson pointed to Cardano’s fee generation, claiming that the network collected just $140,000 in transaction fees over a 30-day period despite ADA carrying a market capitalization of approximately $7.5 billion.

It has been revealed that for him, the disparity raises questions about whether Cardano is attracting enough consumers and developers to sustain its valuation. He believes a blockchain with such a substantial market capitalization should demonstrate considerably stronger usage and demand for its services.

Sources indicate that ultimately, Simpson’s concern is that Cardano needs to translate its technological ambitions and established ecosystem into greater real-world activity. Without a meaningful increase in network usage, he appears unconvinced that ADA offers an attractive investment proposition.

Polygon also made the list, with concerns centered on the growing competition in Ethereum’s scaling ecosystem. Although POL supports a network designed to make transactions faster and cheaper, the increasing number of competing blockchain solutions has made it harder for Polygon to maintain a distinctive advantage.

Simpson’s concern is that newer networks are offering similar benefits, including lower transaction costs and faster processing speeds, leaving Polygon with fewer obvious ways to differentiate itself.

With several projects competing for developers, users, and blockchain activity, POL faces the challenge of proving why it deserves a place ahead of its rivals.

It has been revealed that beyond XRP, Cardano, and Polygon, three other cryptocurrencies also fell short of Ben Simpson’s investment criteria: Sui (SUI), Ronin (RON), and Dogwifhat (WIF). Unlike his concerns about the first three crypto projects, his reservations about these tokens stem largely from changing investment convictions, disappointing adoption, and excessive reliance on market hype.

Sui was among the projects Simpson previously held before changing his investment outlook. The high-speed blockchain is designed to support decentralized applications and transactions, but he eventually dumped his SUI holdings at a loss of between 20% and 30% after his investment thesis changed. He did not elaborate on the specific developments that prompted his decision.

Ronin was another project he abandoned after its growth failed to match his expectations. Initially attracted by the potential of blockchain gaming, the pundit bought into the network, which uses RON for transaction fees and staking. However, the anticipated expansion in gaming adoption did not materialize as he had hoped, prompting him to exit the position relatively quickly. He argued that strong sector potential means little without meaningful retail participation.

Sources indicate that WIF, meanwhile, represented a different kind of investment mistake. Simpson admitted that his decision to buy the Solana-based meme coin was driven largely by hype rather than underlying fundamentals. After his investment thesis changed, he sold his holdings to limit further losses.

His experience with WIF appears to have reinforced his preference for cryptocurrencies backed by stronger fundamentals rather than speculative excitement.

#225287. Tech Report: Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

Tech Report: Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless.
  • In a recent development, few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa.
  • She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months.

In a recent development, few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to.

She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.

But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility.

In a recent development, U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy, younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars.

A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same massive names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers.

“You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural credibility or this idea of being cool,” Izzy Farmiloe, global head of strategy and growth at Dazed Studio, the agency arm of youth culture and fashion publisher Dazed Media, told Fortune.

Long before Instagram gave celebrities a place to document their breakfast, much of the fascination with the cool girl came from how little the public knew about her.

In a November essay for his newsletter, Considered Chaos, brand strategist Eugene Healey explained how each generation’s cool girl was shaped by the media of her time. Kate Moss had fashion magazines, the Olsen twins had the paparazzi, and Alexa Chung had fashion blogs and street-style photographers.

According to recent reports, social media brought audiences closer to the women they admired, making relatability an asset for personalities like Emma Chamberlain. As algorithms began serving up content based on people’s interests rather than simply who they followed, celebrities also had more reason to venture beyond the industries that made them famous.

“Dua Lipa was made for the feed,” Healey wrote.

According to recent reports, her friendship with designer Simon Porte Jacquemus might draw in fashion enthusiasts, while her book club could introduce her to someone who has never listened to Future Nostalgia. Each newly introduced audience offers another opportunity to make money beyond selling records and concert tickets.

It has been revealed that it’s a business model that has become increasingly familiar, with celebrities launching beauty brands, starting newsletters, and inviting followers into their kitchens. Somewhere along the way, having a favorite lip gloss became an opportunity to launch a cosmetics firm.

The trouble with making a living off being cool is that the more people see someone being paid to recommend things, the harder it becomes to tell what she actually likes. Even the seemingly casual Instagram photo dump, filled with blurry pictures and half-eaten meals, can be as carefully curated as the polished posts it was meant to replace.

For Jenna Drenten, a marketing professor at Loyola University Chicago, the problem lies in the very nature of an influencer’s job. “They are expected to sell what is popular, but also expected to discover what’s new,” Drenten told Fortune.

Drenten pointed to BookTok, where recommending a novel outside the usual bestseller rotation can set a creator apart. If enough people take her advice, however, the book becomes just another BookTok sensation, losing some of the very appeal that made it worth recommending in the first place.

Brands risk falling into the same trap. Farmiloe has seen companies chase the same trends and hire the same talent in their pursuit of relevance, spending money only to end up looking more like one another.

“I actually think silence can often be a stronger strategy now,” Farmiloe said.

Trying too hard to look polished may also backfire for brands, especially as artificial intelligence makes it easier to produce everything from flawless images to cultural recommendations. “To sort of show mistakes is a way of proving that a human has made something,” Farmiloe noted, adding that even typos have become chic.

Healey identified three potential successors to the Dua Lipa era: the obsessive, who knows a particular subject inside and out; the ghost, whose reputation spreads without constantly posting; and the host, who brings people together in real life.

It has been revealed that he argued that the three share expertise and charisma that are hard to fake at a moment when faking has never been easier. If the next dominant medium is an AI model that can summarize the world’s knowledge on demand, Healey wrote, cool becomes whatever can’t be summarized.

For brands accustomed to measuring influence in followers, likes, and views, the next cool girl may be much harder to price. Drenten sees growing appeal in people who can offer something beyond a product recommendation, whether it’s a longtime librarian who can introduce readers to literature they might never have discovered on their own or someone who brings strangers together outside the confines of their carefully curated feeds.

As going out becomes increasingly expensive, Farmiloe sees an opportunity for brands to help create those experiences. She pointed to Reference Point, a London library, bookshop, and bar that doubles as a gathering place for chess, poetry, and jazz.

Rather than paying someone to talk about a brand, companies could give people a place to spend time together.

“Instead of just getting noticed, how do you get people to care or actually like engage or spend time with your brand?” Farmiloe said.

According to recent reports, shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

The hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts remarked last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, reveals that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

According to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

The green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

In a recent development, the Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

It has been revealed that since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

In a recent development, the Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

Recent findings suggest that goldman also remarked that retail investors have been buying big tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

It has been revealed that the Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

In the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • In a recent development, in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • It has been revealed that attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

In a recent development, in less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley said that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

It has been revealed that attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals matter ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a new router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal upgrade at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

According to recent reports, A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

On Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

In a recent development, AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says his company’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he stated at the Fresh York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Sources indicate that the FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a manufacturer’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t upgrade for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

There’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Recent findings suggest that former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The headaches just keep piling up for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been on his case about the Commerce Department’s handling of Nvidia, following the news of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy. And now President Trump is blaming his team for publishing “fake” growth numbers before the midterms.“It was just revealed that the real numbers on the economy, published before the election, were fake, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the government agency that does these numbers,” the president posted on Truth Social.

“The American economy under the Trump administration is doing far better than the good numbers already released.”.

The agency Trump appears to be referring to is the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), which sits within the Commerce Department.

The BEA operates with statistical and methodological independence, a safeguard designed to protect the accuracy and impartiality of its statistics.

On Wednesday, the BEA issued revisions to its growth figures for the third quarter of 2026, saying GDP was 4.3%—not the 3.9% it had originally forecast. The upward revision of 0.9% on the initial estimate was “primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending.”.

Industry observers note that analysts are unlikely to be surprised. Revisions are a routine feature of U.S. economic statistics. Lower survey response rates have reduced the precision of some estimates. As UBS’s Pauk Donovan said in a note to clients this morning: “Changes in U.S. economic growth are exaggerated by the fiction of annualization (a technique employed by very few advanced economies).”.

“Data revisions are more common as structural change and poor survey response rates reduce precision.”.

But President Trump suggested there were more nefarious reasons for the near-percentage-point difference in initial estimates to the published figures: “Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.”.

Industry observers note that lutnick issued a bullish economic update. Writing on X, the Commerce Secretary mentioned: “We’re bringing American manufacturing back at a scale nobody thought possible. America’s successes will become even more powerful in the coming years as these projects move from groundbreaking to full production.”.

Trump’s latest clash with federal data agencies could further undermine confidence in U.S. economic statistics. In 2025, the president fired the director of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), Erika McEntarfer, claiming she had overseen the publishing of “phony” job numbers for political reasons. (The president provided no evidence for his claim.).

Sources indicate that this, paired with Trump’s extraordinary attacks on the Federal Reserve under former chairman Jerome Powell, led many economists and investors to worry about the credibility of major U.S. institutions that either inform policy or make it.

At the time, Alberto Cavallo, Professor at Harvard Business School, told Goldman Sachs: “It’s difficult to avoid a comparison to the experience of my home country, Argentina, nearly two decades ago when the president, dismayed at rising inflation, removed statistical agency leadership.

“Some statistics stopped being reported, and official data no longer seemed to align with perceptions. That was a very chaotic period that destroyed trust in Argentina’s official statistics for over a decade.”.

While Cavallo said the U.S. is ahead of some of Argentina’s data bodies in terms of skills and institutional checks and balances, he said the situation was still “very concerning.”.

That doesn’t mean customers are against AI. It means businesses need to think carefully about where they use it and where human support still matters.

Every business was built on a dream, and that’s a deeply human thing. When we replace real care with automation in the moments that matter most, we risk chipping away at the very thing that made the business worth building.

So how do you know where AI belongs and which moments need protecting? Start by asking four questions, then test your answers.

Before using AI in any area of your business, ask these four questions:.

Sources indicate that if a behind-the-scenes task is predictable, simple and low-stakes, let AI handle it. If it’s personal, complex or high-stakes, keep a person in the loop.

Industry observers note that I recently heard from an AnswerConnect client, Craig Grove, founder of GRT Realty, who learned the hard way where not to put AI. He partnered with an AI answering service, only to realize his leads were hanging up on the robot. After switching to human phone answering, he grew his business from six real estate agents to 70.

Running the four questions tells you where AI could go. Testing tells you whether it’s actually working.

I’ve learned firsthand that even the best ideas benefit from a little testing before they’re rolled out more widely. I’m naturally someone who likes to take action, particularly when I’m confident something has potential. After a few instances where the direction or idea I had in mind wasn’t as great as I thought, I found myself in a place where I’d made mistakes.

Industry observers note that in hindsight, I should have started smaller, talked to more people and got feedback first. I’ve never regretted taking a little extra time to test an idea before jumping in. AI deserves the same approach.

Look at it from two angles: your customers and your team.

Then make testing a habit. Things are constantly changing, including your customers’ expectations. What worked in January can fail by June.

According to recent reports, AI is one of the most useful tools business owners have ever had. Used in the right place, it gives your people more time for the work that matters. Used in the wrong place, it erodes the trust your business was built on.

So ask the four questions, test the answers, and keep checking.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • According to recent reports, open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

According to recent reports, open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

According to recent reports, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

In a recent development, for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

It has been revealed that the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Recent findings suggest that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

In a recent development, the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

In a recent development, exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This Saturday, November 28, is Small Business Saturday, the annual post-Thanksgiving tradition that urges holiday shoppers to buy from local, independent businesses. And Eva Longoria wants the people behind those businesses to feel supported all year long.

Industry observers note that “I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making significant decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”.

The actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative launched this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

At the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A new docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

And then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

The stakes are big. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

Recent findings suggest that an analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common complications, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

Recent findings suggest that 1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching fresh customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

Recent findings suggest that “The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she noted. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she said.

3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

“Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she noted.

Sources indicate that 4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

Industry observers note that “You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she stated. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

According to recent reports, to see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the big-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The past weeks have seen the broad crypto ETF market face consistent withdrawals from investors, causing Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, and others to record steady outflows since October.

While the negative trend has continued, Solana has just taken over the leadership in the broad ETF market after recording its first inflow in a while.

Latest data from SosoValue shows that while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP ETFs have continued to struggle with consistent weekly outflows, Solana has just beaten the trend after it finally ended a six-week streak of consecutive weekly outflows.

Notably, the data reveals that Solana spot ETFs have recorded a net inflow of $4.38 million over the week.

Although the net amount of capital received by the ETFs appears decent, it is significant considering the growing crypto market weakness.

While this marks an end to the Solana ETFs' six-week outflow streak, this is the first positive weekly performance they have recorded since October 9.

Further data reveals that Bitcoin spot ETFs suffered the largest withdrawals as investors pulled out about $1.79 billion during the same period.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

#225274. Latest Update: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

Latest Update: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback.
  • Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it.
  • On November 12, Nvidia unveiled that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored.

I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every company whose CEO looks irreplaceable.

The sequence of events tells a story.

On November 12, Nvidia unveiled that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation, after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates.

Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.”.

Then the alternatives fell away. The Financial Times reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day, Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government. Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision.

The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished.

That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options.

A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse.

Accountability depends on a credible alternative. When a board has a successor ready, its questions carry weight, because everyone in the room knows the organization survives if the answers fall short. When it has nobody, the CEO holds the leverage and both sides know it. The duty to oversee him turns into a duty to keep him.

Huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. The board had three decades to prepare for the day he wasn’t there. When that day came, it had a CFO doing two jobs, one outside name, and a market that wanted him back. Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld wrote in Fortune the board had no Plan B.

Investors made the same point from the other side. Within days of the resignation, prominent shareholders were urging the board to keep the door open to Huang. Nobody outside the company had the facts. What they were pricing was a business with no one else to run it.

It has been revealed that the board has since created a national security committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Those are controls on conduct. Neither one is a successor.

It has been revealed that I coach CEOs, and I’ve watched how boards arrive here. Nobody decides to skip succession. It gets postponed, one good quarter at a time.

Over the years a founder’s identity and the organization’s fuse. Raising the question of who comes next starts to feel like disloyalty, so directors leave it for another meeting. The CEO rarely pushes either. Planning your own exit means picturing a company that no longer needs you, and that is the hardest thing to ask of someone whose whole identity is the company.

So both sides stay comfortable. The cost arrives on the one day the board needs a choice and finds it doesn’t have one.

Plenty of boards are living with the same arrangement right now, and it’s invisible for as long as the results are good.

Two tests will tell a director where their board stands.

First, name the person who could run the organization on Monday. One name, already inside the building, whom the top team would follow. If the honest answer is the CFO as caretaker, you have a holding pattern.

Second, recall the last time the board noted no to the CEO on something he cared about. If nobody can remember one, the board has already stopped overseeing him. It just hasn’t been tested yet.

Recent findings suggest that huang may prove to be the right leader for Nvidia’s next chapter. The investigation may answer every open question. Neither would change what the 11 days indicated.

According to recent reports, the board now enters the next crisis in a weaker position than the last one. It has shown its investors, its government and its CEO that it has no alternative to him. He knows it. So does everyone who will ever need to challenge him.

Every director reading this should ask the question Nvidia’s board had to answer in public.

If our CEO were gone tomorrow, would we have a choice?

Industry News: Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The upcoming funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of massive names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

Sources indicate that “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis stated the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a latest startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders remarked the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis stated.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The firm cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The manufacturer isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

According to recent reports, its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders stated. A second, larger site using AMD’s fresh Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The organization notes it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan stated that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a latest AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he mentioned.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

It has been revealed that competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

It has been revealed that coreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Sources indicate that marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The organization’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders remarked. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Recent findings suggest that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe looks to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

It has been revealed that the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis stated. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking tech giant DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

It has been revealed that angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Industry observers note that marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis stated the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one substantial customer that could pull out.

Sources indicate that ultimately, Lewis mentioned he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

Updated at 6:20 a.m. PT with Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO.

Veteran trader Peter Brandt has softened the tone of his recent Bitcoin warnings and remarked on X that the cryptocurrency held at the level it needed to hold after its drop to $55,150 over the weekend.

"Bitcoin held exactly where it had to hold -- for now anyway, but perhaps for more than now," Brandt wrote on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that brandt also shared a monthly chart of Bitcoin together with the post. The chart goes back to 2018, and Brandt marked on it the same patterns that he had already pointed to in previous years. According to the chart, the price of Bitcoin was back above $63,000 at the time of the post and stood at $63,338.

Sources indicate that on Saturday, Bitcoin fell as low as $55,150. It was the lowest price of the cryptocurrency since September 2024, and before that, the lowest price of Bitcoin in 2026 was $57,718 on July 1, according to Coinbase.

On Nov. 15, Brandt posted a weekly chart with a possible head-and-shoulders top and mentioned that, if the pattern proves valid, Bitcoin's October 2025 record of about $126,000 may not be surpassed in his lifetime. Two days before that, on Nov. 13, Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 for the first time since August.

Brandt has also pointed to the history of Bitcoin's bull market cycles more than once. Late last year, he posted a chart showing that each of Bitcoin's five major bull runs began after drawdowns of 75% or more, and he wrote that if the decline carried to $50,000, "the next bull market cycle should carry to $200k to $250K.".

In April, Brandt said that Bitcoin could form an "investable low" in September or October 2026. According to Brandt, this low may or may not go below the February low near $60,000, and the next cycle peak could land between $300,000 and $500,000 in September or October 2029 if the four-year cycle continues to hold.

"Real bottom will not occur until October 2026," Brandt mentioned in an interview in February.

The latest Brandt post comes amid a rally in U.S. tech stocks on Monday. Earlier that day, Nvidia confirmed that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately.

Industry observers note that according to the Nvidia announcement, the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government before the decision, and it is confident that Huang's return "poses no national security risk." Shares of Nvidia surged 33% after the news, according to CNBC.

Bitcoin went up together with tech stocks and briefly climbed above $64,000 on Monday. Before the Nvidia news, Bitcoin had already recovered from the Saturday low to around $61,500.

Industry observers note that huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12. On Nov. 17, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said on the company's earnings call that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A large tech giant had finished moving a group of business customers onto a latest billing platform.
  • Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large tech giant had finished moving a group of business customers onto a latest billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

Recent findings suggest that three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

In a recent development, the affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

Sources indicate that each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation concern while the project remained closed.

The cost showed up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

Team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

The extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

The billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing issues that had nothing to do with the migration.

According to recent reports, as the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

It has been revealed that this is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

Those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

Once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

The sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The firm did three things:.

Those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

In a recent development, the acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

For the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration challenges before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A different pattern surfaced later.

A subset of accounts required manual correction only after a billing adjustment changed how two fields interacted. The migration had passed the stronger acceptance test because the glitch didn’t appear until those accounts went through live billing activity.

Billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the latest exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still revealed a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

Sources indicate that the firm also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

The technical concern was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

Industry observers note that A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

No one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

Sources indicate that that’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow.
  • According to recent reports, around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report.
  • Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Professionals have long been taught a simple formula for career success: work hard, outperform your peers, and bigger paychecks will follow. But this year, employers are planning to reward their star staffers differently; instead of factoring in merit, more companies are considering general pay hikes spread out evenly, dubbed the “peanut butter raises” trend.

According to recent reports, around 44% of employers plan to roll out uniform, across-the-board wage bumps in 2026, according to a 2026 Payscale report. About 16% of organizations are newly implementing these “peanut butter” raises: 9% say they already employ the pay strategy, and another 18% of organizations are considering it this year. And top-performing companies are all-in on the approach. Around 56% of organizations that reported that they would exceed their revenue goals in 2025 are using or actively considering peanut butter pay increases.

Companies are still planning to boost employee pay by 3.5%, the same rate as last year. And while 48% of businesses will continue the tradition of awarding pay bumps based on worker performance—which the report described as a “best practice”—the fresh compensation fad may be trying to alleviate financial headwinds for low-paid workers.

Sources indicate that “Tying merit pay increases to performance ratings has come under criticism in recent years for being too subjective and prone to bias,” the Payscale report noted. “At the same time, some organizations have made headlines by electing to standardize pay increases to alleviate administrative burden and reward workers equally, especially for low wage workers where inflation is a significant concern.”.

In a recent development, job seekers and staffers alike are suffering through a difficult labor market: Hiring has slowed, layoffs are steadily streaming in, and wages don’t feel like they’re holding up. Looking at the year ahead, the picture doesn’t look too pretty.

Wall Street analysts and business executives have been floating the idea we’re in a “K-shaped economy”; higher-income Americans are witnessing their earnings and wealth rise, while lower-income people are struggling against smaller gains and the high cost of living. The concept has come to explain the confusing U.S. economy, where solid overall growth contrasts with sluggish hiring and rising unemployment.

Sources indicate that while U.S. companies are holding their average salary increase budget steady at 3.5%, according to a 2025 report from Willis Towers Watson, there’s a large cohort that is planning to scale back. Nearly a third of businesses strategy to lower their compensation-increase budgets compared to last year, citing a potential recession, dwindling financial performance, and desire for more control over costs.

In a recent development, last year, one high-profile employer ditched its merit-based raises in favor of a general, flat pay bump. Starbucks announced it would be giving a standard 2% raise to all salaried North American employees in 2025, diverging from the norm that managers have a say in the raises of their direct reports. It was all a part of CEO Brian Niccol’s bid to reduce costs in a broader manufacturer turnaround effort.

But Starbucks is just one notable name in a growing list of employers hunkering down for economic hardship. Lexi Clarke, Payscale’s chief people officer, told Fortune last year that pay-increase budgets are being slimmed as tariffs and economic woes create uncertainty, forcing many employers to be on their guard.

“Economic concerns have now overtaken labor competition as the primary driver of compensation decisions,” Clarke said, as “66% of employers cite this as the reason for pulling back, up 17% from last year.”.

Industry observers note that as more companies trim back wage budgets and hand out peanut butter raises, there are many still reinvesting in their star talent. America’s largest private employer, $988 billion retail titan Walmart, unrolled a strategy in 2024 to pay its top store managers up to $620,000 per year.

U.S. CEO John Furner said it was a way to “make managers feel like owners,” acknowledging their success with a slice of the profit pie. Their average base pay was hiked from $130,000 to $160,000, raising their total compensation to between $420,000 and $620,000 annually.

And with more than 4,000 store managers across the U.S. (and around 1.5 million workers) when the policy went into effect, the payout wasn’t just generous—it was a calculated bet on culture.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on February 2, 2026.
