💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

In a recent development, according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

In a recent development, together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

It has been revealed that october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

It has been revealed that at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

According to recent reports, NU7 does not introduce a fresh transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

It has been revealed that the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

According to recent reports, ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who strategy to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

Sources indicate that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Customers need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

Sources indicate that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

In a recent development, that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

In a recent development, the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#225267. Fake Black Friday deals: where the savings come from framing

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4170 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Fake Black Friday deals: where the savings come from framing

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fake Black Friday deals can look like bargains while saving less than promised, from inflated original prices to add-on warranties, padded bundles and minimum-spend shipping.
  • A sale tag only means something next to a reference number, and the retailer usually gets to pick that number.
  • Black Friday lets retailers play that game at scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fake Black Friday deals can look like bargains while saving less than promised, from inflated original prices to add-on warranties, padded bundles and minimum-spend shipping.

A discount isn't a price. It's a comparison. A sale tag only means something next to a reference number, and the retailer usually gets to pick that number. It might be a list price, a "compare at" figure or a price the item carried for a few days back in October. Swap the reference and the same checkout total can pass for a small markdown or a steep one.

Black Friday lets retailers play that game at scale. The day itself falls after U.S. Thanksgiving, which is the fourth Thursday of November, but it stopped being a single day years ago. Promotions now run for weeks, online and in stores, and "early Black Friday" sales often start well before the date.

A fake Black Friday deal is one where the savings come from how the price is presented, not from the price itself. Some lean on a reference price the product almost never sold at. Others push scarcity, swap in a cheaper version of a familiar product or pad the offer with add-ons that aren't worth much. A few just move the cost somewhere else: a monthly installment, a protection proposal, a shipping minimum.

It has been revealed that the Federal Trade Commission has rules against deceptive former-price claims in the U.S. Shoppers don't have to rely on enforcement, though. Price-history trackers, model numbers and the fine print on a promotion usually reveal what a discount is actually worth.

The 10 practices below aren't ranked. Each one is a different way a Black Friday price tag can overpromise, covering price framing, limited stock, lower-spec products, bundles, extended warranties, gift card offers, buy-now-pay-later plans, prices that were already low, last-generation electronics and minimum-spend shipping. For each, we explain how it works, how to spot it and what it can cost you.

According to recent reports, plenty of Black Friday discounts are real, and some are big. The point is to tell the difference between a deal that lowers what you pay and one that just dresses up the same price.

A Black Friday discount is only as real as the original price it is measured against. When the crossed-out figure is set high, or the item rarely sold at it, a large percentage off can describe a modest saving or none at all.

This comparison is known as reference pricing. The struck-through number beside a sale price is the reference point a shopper uses to judge the offer. It might be a list price, a manufacturer's suggested retail price or a regular price from the store's own records.

Those labels do not mean the same thing. The manufacturer's suggested retail price, or MSRP, is a recommendation from the brand. Many products sell below it for much of their time on the market. A discount measured against MSRP can look generous while matching what other stores charge in an ordinary week.

Phrases such as "compare at" and "valued at" work in a similar way. They point to a price at another seller, or to a notional value, rather than a price the shopper would have paid at that store. The tag does not say which seller charged that amount, when it did so or whether anyone bought at it.

The U.S. Federal Trade Commission publishes guidance on former-price comparisons. Its general principle is that an advertised reduction should start from a price the seller genuinely offered. A claim printed on a price tag is still not proof that the original price was real.

Sources indicate that shoppers can check a reference price with price-history tools. Camelcamelcamel and Keepa track prices on Amazon $AMZN listings and display them as charts. A chart demonstrates whether the higher price held for months or appeared only briefly. Both services also offer browser extensions and price-drop alerts.

For items sold outside Amazon, a useful test is the current price of the identical model at several other retailers. If competitors list the same product near the advertised sale price, the percentage off mostly reflects the tag one store chose to display.

The number that decides whether an offer is a bargain is the final price paid, not the size of the markdown. A price below what other sellers charge is a saving whatever percentage appears beside it. A steep percentage off a price few people paid is a framing choice rather than a lower cost.

Industry observers note that A doorbuster is a heavily advertised price that a retailer may stock in very small quantities. Its main job is to bring shoppers into the store or onto the site, where they may buy other items at regular prices.

The strategy behind it is the loss leader. A store accepts a thin margin, or even a loss, on one featured product. It expects to make that back on everything else in the basket. A discounted television can draw in a shopper who then picks up a soundbar, cables, a wall mount and a few unrelated gifts. The advertised price does its work whether or not that shopper ever gets the television.

The limits usually sit in the fine print of the circular or the product page. Phrases such as "while supplies last," "limited quantities" and "no rain checks" signal that the store has made no promise to meet demand. Some ads state a minimum number of units per location. A minimum tells shoppers the store will carry at least that many. It states nothing about how many people will be waiting for them.

Timing adds another restriction. Many doorbusters apply only during a set window, such as the first hours after a store opens or a scheduled online release. Once that window closes or the stock runs out, the same shelf may hold a similar product at a higher price.

That substitution is where the real cost highlights up. A shopper who planned a trip around one price may buy the nearest alternative rather than leave empty-handed. The alternative may be a different brand, a larger size or a model that was never discounted at all.

Before going after a doorbuster, read the quantity and time wording in the ad. Decide in advance what to buy, if anything, if the item sells out. Look up the regular price of a fallback model at other retailers. That reference makes it easier to judge whether the in-store substitute is a real deal or simply the next product on the shelf.

Some TVs, laptops, and other electronics sold for Black Friday are built specifically for the holiday sales rush. They often resemble a brand's regular models but use cheaper components. The low price can reflect a lesser product rather than a real markdown.

These products are sometimes called derivative models. A manufacturer produces a variant of an existing design for a particular retailer or sales event. The outer shell, the brand name and much of the marketing copy can match the familiar version. The differences tend to sit inside.

In TVs, the cuts can show up in the panel and the connections. A made-for-sale set may have fewer HDMI ports, a lower refresh rate or a dimmer, simpler display panel. It may lack features such as local dimming that appear on similar-looking sets from the same brand. Those gaps matter most to buyers who play video games, watch in bright rooms or blueprint to connect several devices.

Recent findings suggest that laptops follow a similar pattern. A holiday version may ship with less memory, a smaller or slower storage drive, a lower-tier processor or a lower-resolution screen. The chassis may use more plastic, and battery capacity can differ. Less memory and storage leave less headroom as software becomes more demanding over the years a laptop is kept.

In a recent development, one common warning sign is an unfamiliar model number. A product that appears at only one retailer, or only during the sales season, may have no regular-price history to compare against. That makes any "was" price hard to judge. It also means reviews of a brand's mainstream model may not describe the product on the shelf.

A shopper can check by copying the exact model number from the listing. The next step is searching for it on the manufacturer's own website and reading the full specification sheet. Comparing that sheet line by line with the brand's standard model in the same size or range shows where the parts differ. A model number that returns no manufacturer page at all is itself useful information.

A made-for-sale product is not automatically a poor buy. A cheaper TV with fewer ports can work in a spare bedroom where only one device is connected. The relevant question is whether the price is low for the product actually in the box, not for the better model it resembles.

A Black Friday bundle saves money only if the shopper would have bought every item in it anyway. When the package includes extras with little use or resale value, the real discount on the main product can shrink to very little.

It has been revealed that retailers and manufacturers build bundles by pairing a headline product with add-ons. A game console might come with a game or a second controller. A camera might ship with a memory card, a bag and a basic tripod. A laptop might include a software subscription, a sleeve or a wireless mouse.

Industry observers note that the advertised bundle value is often the sum of each component's individual list price. That figure can look large on a sign or a product page. It does not show what the shopper would actually pay for those items separately, or whether the shopper wants them at all.

According to recent reports, low-cost accessories are common padding. Cases, screen protectors, charging cables and generic earbuds are widely sold at low prices outside of any sale. Counting them at full list price inflates the stated value of the package.

It has been revealed that bundled games and software need a separate look. A console bundle may include a title the buyer has no interest in, or a download code for an older release. A software subscription may cover only a trial period. Some trials renew at full price unless the buyer cancels.

Industry observers note that bundles also make prices harder to compare. A single product has one price that a shopper can check against other stores. A package of four or five items has no direct equivalent elsewhere. That hides the effective price of the main item.

Recent findings suggest that the practical check is to price the core product on its own at several retailers. Then add only the accessories the buyer would have purchased regardless, at their usual selling prices. If that total is close to or below the bundle price, the bundle offers little extra.

It has been revealed that return terms are worth reading before checkout. Policies for bundles vary by retailer. Some stores may require the entire package back, including every opened accessory, rather than accepting a single item.

According to recent reports, A bundle can still be a reasonable purchase. When every piece fills a real need, buying them together can save time and sometimes money. The test is whether the savings hold up once the unwanted extras are set aside.

Sources indicate that an extended warranty or protection strategy sold at checkout often covers problems the shopper is already protected against. Its price can also cancel out much of the discount that made the item look like a bargain.

Recent findings suggest that most new electronics and appliances come with a manufacturer's warranty. That coverage typically handles defects in materials and workmanship for a set period at no extra cost. A protection strategy bought on the same day usually runs alongside it. The early months of paid coverage can duplicate what the manufacturer already provides.

Sources indicate that legal protections add another layer. In the U.S., most states recognize an implied warranty of merchantability, which requires that a product work for its ordinary purpose. Sellers can disclaim it in some states, so the terms of sale matter. In the U.K., the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives buyers rights to a repair, replacement or refund when goods are faulty. Neither protection requires paying for a separate plan.

It has been revealed that some credit cards also extend the manufacturer's warranty on purchases made with the card. These benefits vary by issuer and by card, and some issuers have reduced or dropped them. A shopper can check the current benefits guide for a specific card before assuming the coverage exists.

The terms of a paid plan set its real value. Many plans exclude accidental damage unless it is listed. They also commonly exclude cosmetic damage, normal wear and misuse. Plans that do cover accidental damage may charge a deductible or service fee for each claim.

It has been revealed that the claims process matters as much as the coverage. Some intends require the owner to ship the device away for repair, leaving them without it for a period. Others may replace a failed product with a refurbished unit rather than a new one. Plans are often run by a third-party administrator rather than by the store itself.

Timing is part of the pitch. A protection plan offered at the register arrives when a shopper has already committed to the purchase and has little time to compare options. Some retailers and manufacturers let buyers add coverage for a period after the sale. The decision does not always have to be made at the counter.

The math takes one step. Subtract the cost of the plan from the advertised saving. The remaining figure is the real discount on the purchase.

Recent findings suggest that A spend-and-get gift card promotion does not lower the price a shopper pays at the register. The bonus card has value only if the shopper returns to the same retailer, spends it before any deadline and follows its terms.

It has been revealed that these Black Friday offers usually follow a simple pattern. A shopper buys a qualifying item or spends past a set amount, and the store hands over a gift card or store credit. The receipt still demonstrates the full sale price. The reward sits on a card that works only at that chain.

Industry observers note that that difference matters when comparing two offers. A direct discount leaves money in a shopper's pocket at checkout. A gift card with the same face value keeps that money inside the retailer's own system. The shopper must make a second purchase to collect any benefit at all.

That second purchase often costs more than the card covers. A gift card rarely matches the exact price of the next item a shopper wants. The shopper pays the difference out of pocket. That extra spending also goes to the same retailer.

Promotional cards can also carry tighter rules than gift cards bought with cash, including earlier expiration dates. Some bonus cards work only during a set redemption window, which may not open until well after the original purchase. Others exclude certain brands, categories or items already on sale.

Recent findings suggest that returns add another complication. A retailer may reduce the refund on a returned item by the value of the bonus card, or ask for the unused card back. A shopper can check the return policy before buying rather than after.

According to recent reports, any balance left unspent stays with the retailer. The industry term for gift card value that never gets redeemed is breakage. That unredeemed value counts in the store's favor, not the shopper's.

Industry observers note that before picking a gift card offer over a cash discount elsewhere, a shopper can weigh three questions. Would they shop at this store again soon anyway? Can they meet the redemption dates? Does the fine print exclude what they proposal to buy next?

In a recent development, splitting a Black Friday purchase into installments through Klarna, Affirm or Afterpay changes when a shopper pays, not how much. A pay-later plan spreads a cost over time. It is not a discount, and in some cases it raises the total a shopper pays.

Retailers often display installment options right next to the sale price. A product listing or checkout page may show a small per-payment figure in large type. The full price may appear nearby in smaller print. That framing can make an expensive television or laptop look cheaper than it is. The total owed stays the same, or grows.

It has been revealed that many short-term plans split a purchase into a handful of equal payments over several weeks. Some of these charge no interest when every payment arrives on time. Longer plans for larger purchases work more like a conventional loan. Some of them charge interest, and the rate depends on the lender, the blueprint and the borrower.

Recent findings suggest that missed payments carry their own costs. Depending on the provider and the proposal, a late payment can bring a fee. Some lenders also run credit checks or report payment history to credit bureaus. A shopper should read the specific terms before agreeing, rather than assume every pay-later plan works the same way.

Stacking looks is a separate risk. Each plan can look manageable on its own. Several plans opened at different stores over one shopping weekend can overlap, though. Those payments may come due in the same weeks and draw on the same bank account or card. One provider's app does not show plans held with other lenders, so the shopper has to track the combined total.

Recent findings suggest that returns add another step. A refund has to move through the lender as well as the retailer. A shopper who sends an item back should confirm with the provider whether scheduled payments pause while the return is processed.

It has been revealed that one check cuts through the framing. Add up the total paid under the proposal and compare it with the upfront price. If the plan adds fees or interest, the Black Friday discount shrinks by that amount. An installment schedule changes the timing of the payments, not what the item costs.

A Black Friday price is not always a latest low. Many advertised Black Friday prices match what the same product cost earlier in the fall. The November tag can simply repeat an earlier offer.

Sources indicate that retailers often attach the Black Friday name to promotions that start early in November. When the same discount carries through to the Friday itself, the date adds a label rather than a lower price. An item at its holiday price in the first week of the month can sit at that figure until the weekend.

In a recent development, other sales events can set an equal or lower mark. Amazon $AMZN's Prime Day, back-to-school promotions and Labor Day sales in the U.S. all cut prices on electronics, appliances and home goods. A price reached at one of those events can match or beat the Black Friday offer on the same item.

A price-history chart shows whether the Black Friday figure has appeared before. For products sold on Amazon, Camelcamelcamel and Keepa chart how a listing's price has moved over time. If the same figure shows up several times earlier in the year, it is a recurring price, not a one-time cut.

This check answers a different question from whether a store's "was" price is genuine. A product can have an honest original price and still hit its holiday sale price several times a year. The useful comparison is with the lowest recent price, not the list price printed beside the discount.

Store policies can also reduce the pressure to buy on a single day. Some retailers match a competitor's lower price. Some refund the difference if their own price drops within a set period after purchase. Terms differ from store to store, and holiday periods can carry separate rules. The current policy is worth reading before checkout.

According to recent reports, prices can shift again after the Friday. Cyber Monday, the Monday after Thanksgiving, brings another round of online discounts. December sales can bring others.

A repeated price is not a bad price. It does mean the Black Friday date adds little urgency. A shopper who misses it may see the same figure at the next major sale event.

Steep Black Friday markdowns on phones, laptops, tablets and game consoles often apply to models that have already been replaced or are about to be. The price cut reflects the product's age in its release cycle, not a one-off act of generosity from the retailer.

Electronics makers refresh many product lines on a fairly regular schedule. Apple $AAPL has introduced most of its new iPhone lineups at events in September. That leaves the previous year's models on shelves in November, beside newer versions that released only weeks earlier.

Retailers and carriers have a reason to clear older inventory before the holiday shopping season ends. A Black Friday promotion is one way to move it.

The listing may not spell any of this out. A product page can describe an item as latest, which is accurate in the sense that it is unopened and unused. That word notes nothing about when the model first went on sale. A shopper who sees a large discount on a laptop may not realize its processor belongs to a chip generation that has since been superseded.

In a recent development, A few checks can establish a model's age. The manufacturer's website usually lists the current lineup, and a model missing from it has likely been discontinued. Product reviews and manufacturers' press pages give the date a model first went on sale.

Industry observers note that the trade-offs go beyond raw speed. Phones and tablets depend on software updates for security fixes and new features. Every device eventually stops receiving those updates. An older model reaches that cutoff sooner than a newer one bought on the same day.

Recent findings suggest that many manufacturers publish enhancement policies for their recent devices, and those pages show how long support is promised. Older hardware may also lack newer ports, wireless standards or camera features that later models added.

Recent findings suggest that A last-generation device can still suit a buyer who wants a capable phone or laptop at a lower price and does not need the newest features. The useful comparison is between the discounted older model and the current one. That means weighing the gap in price against the gap in specs and the years of software support each has left.

A free shipping offer that applies only above a minimum order total can cost more than it saves. If reaching the threshold means adding items a shopper did not plan to buy, the extra spending can exceed the delivery fee it was meant to avoid.

In a recent development, the mechanics are straightforward. A retailer sets an order value at which shipping charges drop away. A shopper whose cart sits just below that line faces a choice. They can pay for delivery, or they can add something to cross the line. The threshold works for the retailer when shoppers take the second path.

Industry observers note that the added item is the part to examine. Online stores often show low-cost products near the cart or checkout page, such as socks, phone chargers, batteries or small household goods. These fillers make it easy to close the gap. Whether that counts as a saving depends on whether the shopper needed the item.

Recent findings suggest that A quick comparison settles the question. Set the shipping fee against the price of the filler item. If the filler costs more than the fee and serves no real need, paying for delivery is the cheaper outcome. If the filler was already on the shopping list, crossing the threshold can make sense.

Several alternatives can remove the threshold from the decision. Many large chains let shoppers buy online and pick up in store, generally without a delivery charge. Some retailers sell paid memberships that include free shipping without an order minimum. That membership fee pays off only for shoppers who order often enough to offset it. A retailer's threshold during a holiday promotion may also differ from its usual one.

Returns deserve a look before checkout. Free outbound shipping does not guarantee free return shipping. Some retailers deduct a return shipping fee or a restocking charge from refunds. Those policies can vary by product category. A filler item that ends up being sent back may cost the shopper money twice.

The threshold itself is a pricing tool rather than a discount. It encourages larger orders. Each delivery then carries more merchandise, which spreads the retailer's shipping cost across a bigger sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he remarked most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which states it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

In a recent development, his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

In a recent development, he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he noted. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google revealed a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, remarked he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a substantial technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Sources indicate that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the manufacturer for a briefing.

Sources indicate that smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate organization, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and mentioned the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for challenges it considered key.

Industry observers note that outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he noted much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Industry observers note that smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

  • Sources indicate that A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three fresh priorities competing for specialist capacity.
  • According to recent reports, the planning baseline also showed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the new year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three fresh priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

According to recent reports, the planning baseline also showed an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the new year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

In a recent development, during the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the fresh priorities to start as planned. The program lead remarked the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

What the planning discussion didn’t do was force the remediation work to compete again with the three newly introduced priorities. It sat in the baseline as committed work, while leaders debated how to allocate what they believed was the remaining capacity.

By the end of the session, the team had made disciplined choices:.

The overcommitment was already there.

Sources indicate that the problem became visible in the first weeks of execution. One of the approved priorities needed several of the same risk, legal and data specialists who were still closing the remediation program.

The planning model counted those people as partially available because the older work was expected to wind down early in the year. Instead, a final set of regulatory findings required more analysis, and a small group of specialists stayed fully engaged.

The new priority still had its approved funding, executive sponsor and start date. The people needed to move it weren’t actually free.

The old work was visible, but its claim on the new year’s capacity had been treated as fixed background rather than as a choice.

Managers began stretching the same specialists across both commitments. The new priority’s first milestone slipped as specialist reviews that should have happened early were pushed behind remediation work. Meetings multiplied, decisions slowed, and work that looked fully staffed on paper started moving in fragments.

The pressure spread beyond those specialists. Project leads started moving milestones to fit the people they could get, finance held back some spending because dependent work couldn’t start, and senior leaders spent more time resolving clashes between commitments they believed had already been reconciled during planning.

The interesting thing was that the approved strategy hadn’t changed, but the amount of work that could move at the same time already had.

It has been revealed that the new initiative hadn’t been badly prioritized at all. The leadership team had already removed a lower-ranked proposal, but part of the capacity used in the ranking exercise simply hadn’t been available to begin with.

This is where the “Hidden Problems” execution leak appears.

The planning process had surfaced the remediation program, its budget and its expected completion date, yet the latest work was still being ranked against an overstated view of what remained available.

A baseline records what’s already in motion, but it doesn’t force old work to justify its capacity against latest work. Once carryover is treated as given, only the new initiatives are asked to compete.

That distinction matters because visibility can create false confidence.

Leaders can see every major piece of work on one page and still never face the question of whether an old commitment deserves to keep the people and budget it carried across the year boundary.

Listing carryover isn’t the same as choosing it again. The planning process therefore becomes disciplined about one side of the load while leaving the other side untouched.

According to recent reports, when execution starts slowly, leadership tightens prioritization. Leaders ask for fewer initiatives, sharper business cases and clearer ranking, then delay or reject latest proposals that can’t justify scarce capacity.

Those actions improve the choices among new priorities; however, they don’t reopen the older commitments already sitting in the baseline. That was the pattern in this business unit.

Leadership had reduced the newly introduced-priority list before approving the plan, and when capacity pressure appeared, the first response was to ask whether one of the new initiatives should move more slowly.

The remediation program wasn’t part of that debate because it had been approved in the prior year, and finishing it was treated as an “obligation” rather than as a competing use of scarce capacity.

The organization was re-ranking newly introduced work while the carryover never faced the same test.

Industry observers note that A stronger planning process adds a formal carryover line. That certainly improves visibility, but it doesn’t change the underlying mechanism when carryover remains exempt from comparison.

The remediation work can appear clearly in the plan, with its budget, owner and expected completion date, and still never face the one central question: Is finishing this work now more valuable than starting the upcoming priority that needs the same people?

Industry observers note that in this business unit, the remediation program remained on every planning view. Its existence was never hidden. What did stay hidden was the effect of treating its capacity claim as “non-negotiable” while the new priorities competed for whatever was left.

The plan could be complete as an inventory and incomplete as a capacity decision.

Every item appeared somewhere, but not every item had to earn its place in the same contest for scarce people and budget.

It has been revealed that by the time the conflict became obvious, leaders were dealing with a problem the planning process had already created. The remediation work couldn’t simply stop, and the fresh priority had already been approved.

The same scarce specialists now sat between two legitimate commitments, each with consequences for delay. Leaders were forced to make the tradeoff during execution instead of during planning, when they still had more room to change the portfolio.

Industry observers note that when that conflict reached the next leadership review, the discussion was no longer about which work deserved to start. It was about which already-approved commitment would lose access to people both sides now depended on.

The proposal didn’t fail because leaders chose the wrong new priorities. Not at all. The planning choice had been postponed until both commitments were already in motion.

#225263. Industry News: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1185 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 latest articles.
  • “Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes.
  • I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 latest articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last.

“Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work.

I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom.

Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces.

At Bergens Tidende, known as BT, reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one.

It has been revealed that vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he notes the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most vital point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way.

Office workers describe something different. In a Workday survey of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by researchers at BetterUp and Stanford, each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows.

A Georgia Tech researcher argued this month that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking.

Industry observers note that johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster.

Recent findings suggest that on one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson mentioned. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less vital.

A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice.

So has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published.

Recent findings suggest that I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025 master’s thesis at Aalto University made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.”.

Recent findings suggest that for companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable.

As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.

Ethereum bulls face a frightening downside scenario after legendary trader and classical chart analyst Peter Brandt issued a fresh warning that the second-largest cryptocurrency could collapse below $500. His bearish outlook has raised fresh concerns about ETH’s ability to withstand mounting selling pressure, particularly as market uncertainty continues to weigh on investor sentiment.

In a November 24 post on X, Peter Brandt pointed to Ethereum’s deteriorating weekly chart structure, suggesting that ETH is approaching a critical point within a multi-year consolidation pattern.

Recent findings suggest that the weekly chart above shows a large symmetrical triangle that has formed over several market cycles. Its upper boundary is defined by a descending resistance line stretching from Ethereum’s November 2021 peak near $4,800, while the lower boundary consists of an ascending support line originating around the 2022 bear-market bottom.

Together, these converging trendlines have gradually narrowed Ethereum’s trading range, setting the stage for a potentially decisive breakout or breakdown.

ETH briefly broke above the triangle’s upper resistance during its 2025 rally, eventually reaching a latest all-time high near $4,954 in August. However, the bullish breakout failed to produce a sustained upward move, with the cryptocurrency subsequently reversing direction.

The resulting decline has produced a series of lower highs and renewed selling pressure throughout 2026, bringing ETH increasingly close to the triangle’s lower boundary.

Brandt’s bearish outlook hinges on Ethereum losing its long-standing ascending support trendline, a development that could undermine a chart structure that has supported several significant recovery attempts since 2022.

Using $1,648 as the current reference price, ETH would need to shed approximately 16.1% to revisit the critical $1,383 support level. However, the classical chartist’s more alarming outlook points to a potential plunge below $500 if the cryptocurrency fails to defend this structural floor.

It has been revealed that A drop from $1,648 to $500 would translate into a staggering 69.7% decline. Even if ETH first falls to $1,383, it would still face another 63.8% downside before reaching $500.

This distinction is key because the sub-$500 projection represents a much deeper bearish scenario, not an automatic consequence of losing the immediate support level.

Such a collapse would also push Ethereum below its 2022 bear-market low, potentially marking a dramatic breakdown in its longer-term price structure.

According to recent reports, for Ethereum to begin reversing its bearish momentum, buyers must first push the altcoin king back above $1,715 and sustain a recovery beyond that threshold. Reclaiming this level would signal improving demand and offer an early sign that selling pressure is easing.

Recent findings suggest that the next major hurdle sits around $1,840, which coincides with ETH’s November 23 rebound high. A decisive move above this resistance would help invalidate the recent pattern of lower highs and strengthen the case for a broader recovery.

On the downside, a confirmed weekly close below $1,383—particularly if followed by an unsuccessful attempt to reclaim that level—would signal a potentially damaging breakdown of Ethereum’s multi-year ascending support structure. If that scenario unfolds, ETH could face renewed selling pressure toward the psychologically important $1,000 mark. A deeper deterioration in market conditions could then bring Brandt’s sub-$500 projection into sharper focus.

However, the bearish forecast remains conditional rather than inevitable. Ethereum has yet to lose the critical $1,383 support, leaving its ability to defend this level central to determining whether Brandt’s worst-case scenario becomes a reality.

From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary rolled out his firm a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary rolled out his firm a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a latest line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary noted, which benefits everyone.

It has been revealed that just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

Sources indicate that high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the challenges.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

In a recent development, when I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there rapidly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

Sources indicate that that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

Sources indicate that my personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally crucial: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

In a recent development, I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do massive things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

Sources indicate that AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as substantial an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

#225259. I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary.
  • Sources indicate that after it started, creative quality dropped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

Sources indicate that after it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target remarked completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those indicates up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the initiative asked for.

Industry observers note that I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

It has been revealed that for a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

We traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

Recent findings suggest that when we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. Upcoming editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

According to recent reports, that changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

It has been revealed that I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

Industry observers note that A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

According to recent reports, bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

Recent findings suggest that we stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

The results came swiftly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

Recent findings suggest that the difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

It has been revealed that we’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

The early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

According to recent reports, while the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

It has been revealed that if you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

In a recent development, the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

Recent findings suggest that after it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

Sources indicate that the target mentioned completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the strategy asked for.
